title: Real beauty
hookLine: to a young man with elaborate hair: beauty is in excellence, not in grooming (Discourses 3.1)
carry: you're your will, your choosing self

cards: A young student of public speaking came to the Stoic teacher Epictetus with his hair dressed more elaborately than usual, his whole appearance polished to a shine. Should a teacher say something? Epictetus weighs it.
If I keep quiet, he reasons, this young man may someday say: Epictetus saw me like that, and never said a word. So he speaks. But he doesn't mock.
He asks a question about dogs and horses.

teach.b: This is Discourses book three, chapter one. Tell me, Epictetus says to the young man, don't you think some dogs are beautiful? Some horses?
Yes. Is it the same thing that makes each of them beautiful, or something different? A dog is beautiful when it's excellent as a dog, a horse when it's excellent as a horse.

teach.h: EXCELLENT AT BEING WHAT IT IS.
teach.b: A beautiful racehorse and a beautiful sheepdog aren't beautiful in the same way; each is beautiful by being very good at being what it is. So what makes a human being beautiful? Excellence as a human.
And what is that? Justice. Moderation.
Self-control. If you want to be beautiful, Epictetus tells him, work on those. Then comes the line that turns a lecture into a kindness.
You aren't your hair, he says, or your skin. You're your will, your choosing self. Make that beautiful, and you will be beautiful.
He's not against looking after yourself. Elsewhere in the Discourses he's quite firm that students should keep clean and not put people off.
His point is about where the real work goes. A morning in front of the mirror shapes the hair. A morning of being honest, patient and fair shapes the person.
Only one of those, for Epictetus, is the beauty that belongs to a human being.

how: Some readers of this chapter make a point of praising others for their character rather than their appearance, and give their own mornings to character as well as grooming.

o: a face that looks lovely without any makeup
good looks that last well into old age
excellence at being human: justice and self-control

s: Epictetus mocks the young man's hair in front of the class
he asks him a gentle question about dogs and horses.
he says each creature is beautiful by being excellent at what it is
a dog as a dog, a horse as a horse, a human as a human.
Epictetus tells his students not to bother keeping clean
elsewhere he insists they keep clean; his point is where the real work goes.

games.q: you're Epictetus. a student walks in with elaborately styled hair. what do you do?
o: ask him what makes a dog or a horse beautiful.
games.why: he worried the young man would one day say Epictetus never told him, so he asked about dogs and horses, and led him to human excellence.

practice: Think of someone you know who is beautiful in Epictetus' sense: honest, kind, steady, fair. Picture their face, and ask what makes it beautiful to you, the features or the person behind them.
Then ask, quietly, which of those qualities you'd like someone to see in you.

wordCard.voice: Real beauty. Epictetus to a carefully groomed young man: each creature is beautiful by excelling at what it is, and a human's excellence is justice and self-control.

orig.note: Greek kallos: beauty (as in calligraphy, beautiful writing); 3.1 asks what makes each creature beautiful.

carryVoice: Your line: you're your will, your choosing self. That's where the beauty lives. Day four hundred sixteen, done.
